newsitem.title: USA: Food aid undermined N.Korea barter deal - U.S. firm.
newsitem.headline: Food aid undermined N.Korea barter deal - U.S. firm.

text.p: A wheat-for-zinc barter with North Korea foundered because food aid was donated and Pyongyang wanted to use the zinc elsewhere, the chairman of the U.S. grain-trading giant Cargill Inc. said on Thursday.

After a Senate Agriculture Committee hearing on food security in Africa, Ernie Micek told reporters Cargill still hoped to sell grain to North Korea, adding: "As far as we are concerned, the door is open."

Cargill received permission early this year to sell up to 500,000 metric tons of food grains to North Korea. A barter of 20,000 metric tons of wheat for 5,000 metric tons of zinc was reached in April but fell apart in June, just before delivery.

"I think they did that because they received considerable free aid from a number of countries and aid groups around the world and they decided the limited barter materials that they had, in this case zinc, they wanted to use in some other means," Micek said.
Traders in Asia suggested at the time that North Korea might not have had enough zinc on hand or decided to sell metal directly to reap attractive prices.

Asked about the potential for future barters, perhaps with other metals, Micek said North Korea could not deliver large quantities. "The number of commodities they have available for barter is very limited," he said.
The U.N. food agency the World Food Programme appealed this month for $46 million to feed North Korean children.

At a Washington news conference earlier on Thursday, WFP executive director Catherine Bertini said about 75 percent of this money had been raised. An appeal for $96 million earlier this year had already been covered by donors.
Bertini said the WFP estimated there was a shortfall of between 700,000 and 800,000 metric tons of food.
